{{Short description|Algebraic topology theory}}
In [[mathematics]], '''equivariant cohomology''' (or ''Borel cohomology'') is a [[cohomology theory]] from [[algebraic topology]] which applies to [[topological space]]s with a [[Group action (mathematics)|group action]].  It can be viewed as a common generalization of [[group cohomology]] and an ordinary [[cohomology theory]].

If <math>G</math> acts freely, then the equivariant cohomology ring is just the singular cohomology ring of the quotient space <math>X / G</math>. In particular, if <math>G</math> is the [[trivial group]], then the equivariant cohomology ring is the ordinary [[cohomology ring]] of <math>X</math>. If <math>X</math> is [[contractible]], it reduces to the cohomology ring of the [[classifying space]] <math>BG</math> (that is, the group cohomology of <math>G</math> when <math>G</math> is finite.)

== Definitions ==
Let <math>X</math> be a topological space, with a (left) action by a group <math>G</math>{{Clarify|reason=Can G be any group or must it be a topological group?|date=December 2025}}. Let <math>EG</math> be a contractible space with a free (right) action by the same group. Define <math>EG \times_G X</math> to be the quotient space <math>(EG \times X) / {\sim}</math>, where the equivalence relation <math>\sim</math> identifies <math>(e \cdot g, x)</math> with <math>(e, g \cdot x)</math> for all <math>e \in EG, x \in X, g \in G</math>. The equivariant cohomology ring of <math>X</math> (with respect to the group <math>G</math>) is then defined as the singular cohomology ring of this space:<ref>{{Cite book |last=Anderson |first=David |title=Equivariant Cohomology in Algebraic Geometry |last2=Fulton |first2=William |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2023 |isbn=9781009349994 |page=1}}</ref><math display="block">H^*_G(X) := H^*(EG \times_G X).</math>The space <math>EG \times_G X</math> is known as the '''Borel construction''', or '''[[homotopy quotient]]'''. Projection onto the first factor gives it the structure of a [[Fiber bundle|fibre bundle]] over the classifying space <math>BG</math>. This is the [[associated bundle|associated]] <math>X</math>-bundle obtained from the action of <math>G</math> on <math>X</math> and the [[principal bundle]] <math>EG \to BG</math>. The bundle <math>X \to EG \times_G X \to BG</math> is called the Borel fibration.

The group cohomology ring of <math>G</math> can be recovered by taking <math>X</math> to be a point, as in this case the homotopy quotient is just the classifying space of <math>G</math>. If <math>G</math> acts freely on <math>X</math>, then the canonical map <math>EG \times_G X \to X/G</math> is a homotopy equivalence and so one gets <math display="inline">H_G^*(X) = H^*(X/G).</math>

It is also possible to define the equivariant cohomology <math>H_G^*(X;A)</math> of <math>X</math> with coefficients in a <math>G</math>-module ''A''; these are [[abelian group]]s. This construction is the analogue of cohomology with local coefficients.

If ''X'' is a [[manifold]], ''G'' a [[compact Lie group]] and coefficients are taken in the field of real numbers or the field of complex numbers (the most typical situation), then the above cohomology may be computed using the so-called [[Cartan model]] (see [[equivariant differential form]]s.)

The construction should not be confused with other cohomology theories, such as [[Bredon cohomology]] or the cohomology of [[invariant differential form]]s: if ''G'' is a compact Lie group, then, by the averaging argument{{Citation needed|reason=Previous link was incorrect.|date=October 2017}}, any form may be made invariant; thus, cohomology of invariant differential forms does not yield new information.

[[Koszul duality]] is known to hold between equivariant cohomology and ordinary cohomology.

=== Relation with groupoid cohomology ===
For a [[Lie groupoid]] <math>\mathfrak{X} = [X_1 \rightrightarrows X_0]</math> equivariant cohomology of a smooth manifold<ref>{{harvnb|Behrend|2004}}</ref> is a special example of the groupoid cohomology of a Lie groupoid. This is because given a <math>G</math>-space <math>X</math> for a compact Lie group <math>G</math>, there is an associated groupoid<blockquote><math>\mathfrak{X}_G = [G\times X \rightrightarrows X] </math></blockquote>whose equivariant cohomology groups can be computed using the Cartan complex <math>\Omega_G^\bullet(X)</math> which is the totalization of the de-Rham double complex of the groupoid. The terms in the Cartan complex are<blockquote><math>\Omega^n_G(X) = \bigoplus_{2k+i = n}(\text{Sym}^k(\mathfrak{g}^\vee)\otimes \Omega^i(X))^G</math></blockquote>where <math>\text{Sym}^\bullet(\mathfrak{g}^\vee)</math> is the [[symmetric algebra]] of the dual Lie algebra from the Lie group <math>G</math>, and <math>(-)^G</math> corresponds to the <math>G</math>-invariant forms. This is a particularly useful tool for computing the cohomology of <math>BG</math> for a compact Lie group <math>G</math> since this can be computed as the cohomology of<blockquote><math>[G \rightrightarrows *]</math></blockquote>where the action is trivial on a point. Then,<blockquote><math>H^*_{dR}(BG) = \bigoplus_{k\geq 0 }\text{Sym}^{2k}(\mathfrak{g}^\vee)^G</math></blockquote>For example,<blockquote><math>\begin{align}
H^*_{dR}(BU(1)) &= \bigoplus_{k=0}\text{Sym}^{2k}(\mathbb{R}^\vee) \\
&\cong \mathbb{R}[t] \\
&\text{ where } \deg(t) = 2
\end{align}</math></blockquote>since the <math>U(1)</math>-action on the dual Lie algebra is trivial.

== An example of a homotopy quotient ==
The following example is Proposition 1 of [http://www.math.harvard.edu/~lurie/282ynotes/LectureIV-Approaches.pdf].

Let ''X'' be a complex projective [[algebraic curve]]. We identify ''X'' as a topological space with the set of the complex points <math>X(\mathbb{C})</math>, which is a compact [[Riemann surface]]. Let ''G'' be a complex simply connected semisimple Lie group. Then any principal ''G''-bundle on ''X'' is isomorphic to a trivial bundle, since the [[classifying space]] <math>BG</math> is [[n-connected|2-connected]] and ''X'' has real dimension 2. Fix some smooth ''G''-bundle <math>P_\text{sm}</math> on ''X''. Then any principal ''G''-bundle on <math>X</math> is isomorphic to <math>P_\text{sm}</math>. In other words, the set <math>\Omega</math> of all isomorphism classes of pairs consisting of a principal ''G''-bundle on ''X'' and a complex-analytic structure on it can be identified with the set of complex-analytic structures on <math>P_\text{sm}</math> or equivalently the set of holomorphic connections on ''X'' (since connections are integrable for dimension reason). <math>\Omega</math> is an infinite-dimensional complex affine space and is therefore contractible.

Let <math>\mathcal{G}</math> be the group of all automorphisms of <math>P_\text{sm}</math> (i.e., [[gauge group]].) Then the homotopy quotient of <math>\Omega</math> by <math>\mathcal{G}</math> classifies complex-analytic (or equivalently algebraic) principal ''G''-bundles on ''X''; i.e., it is precisely the classifying space <math>B\mathcal{G}</math> of the discrete group <math>\mathcal{G}</math>.

One can define the [[moduli stack of principal bundles]] <math>\operatorname{Bun}_G(X)</math> as the [[quotient stack]] <math>[\Omega/\mathcal{G}]</math> and then the homotopy quotient <math>B\mathcal{G}</math> is, by definition, the [[homotopy type]] of <math>\operatorname{Bun}_G(X)</math>.

== Equivariant characteristic classes ==
Let ''E'' be an [[equivariant vector bundle]] on a ''G''-manifold ''M''. It gives rise to a vector bundle <math>\widetilde{E}</math> on the homotopy quotient <math>EG \times_G M</math> so that it pulls-back to the bundle <math>\widetilde{E}=EG \times E</math> over <math>EG \times M</math>. An equivariant [[characteristic class]] of ''E'' is then an ordinary characteristic class of <math>\widetilde{E}</math>, which is an element of the completion of the cohomology ring <math>H^*(EG \times_G M) = H^*_G(M)</math>. (In order to apply [[Chern–Weil theory]], one uses a finite-dimensional approximation of ''EG''.)

Alternatively, one can first define an equivariant [[Chern class]] and then define other characteristic classes as invariant polynomials of Chern classes as in the ordinary case; for example, the equivariant [[Todd class]] of an equivariant line bundle is the [[Todd function]] evaluated at the equivariant first Chern class of the bundle. (An equivariant Todd class of a line bundle is a [[power series]] (not a polynomial as in the non-equivariant case) in the equivariant first Chern class; hence, it belongs to the completion of the equivariant cohomology ring.)

In the non-equivariant case, the first Chern class can be viewed as a [[bijection]] between the set of all isomorphism classes of [[complex line]] bundles on a manifold ''M'' and <math>H^2(M; \mathbb{Z}).</math><ref>using [[Čech cohomology]] and the isomorphism <math>H^1(M; \mathbb{C}^*) \simeq H^2(M; \mathbb{Z})</math> given by the [[exponential function|exponential map]].</ref> In the equivariant case, this translates to: the equivariant first Chern gives a bijection between the set of all isomorphism classes of equivariant complex line bundles and <math>H^2_G(M; \mathbb{Z})</math>.

== Localization theorem ==
{{expand-section|date=April 2014}}
{{main|Localization formula for equivariant cohomology}}
The localization theorem is one of the most powerful tools in equivariant cohomology.
